$comment: Committed thresholds. A metric that drops below its floor (or above its ceiling) fails
the build exactly like a unit test. Raising a floor is a normal PR; lowering one needs
an ADR saying why the system got worse and that we accepted it.
Measured on the labelled set built by withholding Schedule I recipient EINs.
Precision is weighted far above recall on purpose: a wrong link corrupts every
downstream signal for that funder, while a missed link only costs coverage, and the
record still counts toward funder-side statistics.
Floors set from the fitted operating point (link 0.80, reject 0.70, margin 0.08),
verified on a held-out half of the labelled set at 98.1% precision and 65.7% recall
with 8.5% routed to review -- see evals/link-threshold-curve.json and ADR-0009. The
floors sit a little under the measurement so ordinary corpus-to-corpus drift is not
a build failure, while a real regression is.
For organisations already in the graph with known funders, hide their real funders and
measure whether the recommender surfaces them in the top 50. This is the central claim
of the product made testable without waiting for a user to apply and hear back.
Measured at 32.1% mean recall@50 across all 12 organisations in the sample on the
2025 corpus. The floor sits under that to absorb corpus drift, not to excuse a
regression.
organisations_measured_floor exists because the sample used to shrink in silence: a
parse failure dropped 7 of 12 and the mean was reported over whatever survived. The
number a mean is taken over is part of the result, so it is asserted like any other.
Parse faults are rows in a grant table that could not be turned into a record.
Reconciliation divergence is 990-PF filings whose itemised rows differ from their own
stated total by more than 1%.
The bar set before any data was ingested: a $656k literacy council in Wilmington NC
must surface at least 15 credible funders. Cleared on 17% of one year's data during
validation (validation/RESULTS.txt), so this is a floor, not a hope.
